vignette: Leilani was 28 years old when the soldiers came through her village market in the islands. She had been buying fish for her grandmother's birthday, and the morning was bright and ordinary. Then the gunfire started, and she threw herself behind a stack of crates. From that cramped space she could smell sweat-the soldiers' bodies, thick and close-and the metallic tang of fear rising from her own skin. When she dared to look, she saw a man fall a few feet away, his eyes still open, and that image burned into her mind like a photograph she could never put down. She managed to run when the soldiers moved on, but she never forgot the way the odour clung to her clothes for days afterward. Now, at 75, Leilani works as an auditor for a county office in California. She is married to a kind, quiet man named Tui, who has learned not to startle her. She sought help because the memories had become unbearable-triggered not only by the smell of heavy sweat in a crowded elevator but also by moments she once would have welcomed. When she feels genuinely happy or relaxed, even briefly, the sense of safety collapses. That pleasant feeling somehow reminds her of the morning before the attack, and then the olfactory recall swells-the sour, urgent smell of bodies pressing toward death-and she is back behind the crates, unable to find words to tell anyone what she is reliving. And after the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me. The triggers also drag her into a spiral of negative appraisals. When a colleague's body odour reaches her in a meeting, Leilani becomes convinced that others can see what happened to her just by looking at her-that her face is a map of the horror. She has come to believe she will never feel normal emotions again, that the part of her that could laugh without reservation is dead. That belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost. Some days she wonders if her life is still worth living. She keeps these thoughts to herself, but they press harder each time she is forced into the workplace, where the fluorescent lights feel like interrogation lamps and every new face might be a threat. That feeling of exposure feeds her threat behaviours. In the office she always chooses a desk with her back to a wall, scanning the room before she sits. She frequently looks behind her when walking to the break room, checking if someone is following. And she has started taking unnecessary risks-crossing streets without looking, driving faster than she should-as if daring the world to finish what the soldiers started. These threat responses, in turn, sharpen her memory. The moment she feels her back exposed, the photographic recall flashes: the soldier's boots, the dead man's staring eyes. The olfactory memory hits again, and she is trapped. She has developed elaborate strategies to manage the chaos. She ruminates endlessly about how the event could have been prevented-if she had stayed home, if she had gone to the other end of the market. She goes over and over why it happened to her, as if finding the right answer would lift the weight. Before any interaction, even a phone call, she rehearses what to say, running the conversation in her head until it feels safe. But these strategies misfire. The rumination about prevention only brings the memory into sharper focus, making the olfactory and photographic details more vivid. To stop the memory from overwhelming her, she started going over the event again and again in her mind, searching for ways it could have been prevented-a strategy that only made the details more vivid and the sense of helplessness deeper. Rehearsing conversations reinforces her belief that she is broken, that she must script her words because her real self is too damaged to trust. And the constant mental preparation keeps her in a state of high threat arousal-she is always alert, always scanning, always ready. At home, Leilani has grown distant. Tui tries to hold her hand, but she flinches because she cannot bear the feeling of skin touching skin-it reminds her of the soldiers' bodies. She has stopped attending church, where the smell of incense and crowds used to be her comfort. Her world has shrunk to the corner of the living room where she sits with her back against the wall, watching the door. What finally brought her to seek help was a night when she stood in the kitchen, holding a knife, and whispered to herself that she was not sure her life was worth living anymore. Tui heard her and wept. She came to the clinic because she is terrified of what she might do-and because somewhere, beneath the ruin, she still hopes to find the woman who once bought fish in the morning sun without fear.
